findings: The Lattimore–Szepesvári adversarial model fixes reward vectors x_t in [0,1]^k and measures expected regret over learner action randomization against the best fixed arm. Exp3 uses the loss-based unbiased estimator 1-1{A_t=i}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}, not the unbounded gain estimator 1{A_t=i}X_t/P_{t,i}; its conditional second moment/variance carries the 1/P_{t,i} factor.

Theorem 11.2 gives eta=sqrt(2 log(k)/(nk)) and expected regret at most sqrt(2nk log k). The full source proof uses a one-sided exponential inequality and the estimator's second-moment bound; the generic bounded-loss Hedge regret theorem does not apply to these importance-weighted values.

The source states that expected-regret algebra extends to reward vectors chosen from past history before the current action, while its policy-regret note shows current-action-dependent rewards can defeat the fixed-arm policy benchmark. The scaffold separates those adversary models and makes no Exp3-IX high-probability claim; the IX proof is an exercise.

findings: The source's contextual bandit with expert advice uses k actions, M experts each reporting a probability vector before the round, and an obliviously fixed reward vector in [0,1]^k. Experts' advice is independent of learner actions; regret is expected against the best single fixed expert.

Exp4 forms P_t=Q_t E(t), samples an arm, uses the gamma=0 loss-based importance estimator, propagates estimated arm rewards through each expert vector, and exponentiates expert weights. Theorem 18.1 gives eta=sqrt(2 log(M)/(nk)) and expected regret at most sqrt(2nk log M).

The theorem proof invokes Lemma 18.2, whose proof is Exercise 18.2. Exp4-IX with gamma>0 and high-probability analysis is Exercise 18.3; the scaffold records the theorem contract without attributing these omitted proofs to the textbook.

findings: The source model is linear reward r(c,a)=<theta*,psi(c,a)> with conditionally 1-subgaussian noise given the history/context/action before reward. In linear-bandit notation, actions are predictable feature vectors; the context-action formulation is a special case.

The regularized estimate is theta_hat_t=V_t^{-1}sum_{s<=t} A_s X_s, V_t=lambda I+sum_{s<=t}A_s A_s^T, with lambda>0. Theorem 20.5 gives a simultaneous radius sqrt(lambda)||theta*|| + sqrt(2 log(1/delta)+log(det(V_t)/lambda^d)); this is locally carried into beta_t as a squared-radius parameter.

Theorem 19.2 additionally requires nondecreasing beta_t>=1, feature norms <=L, and per-round optimal-mean range <=1. It gives the exact high-probability pseudo-regret bound sqrt(8 n beta_n log(det V_n/det V_0)) and the trace/AM-GM bound sqrt(8 d n beta_n log(1+n L^2/(d lambda))). The expected-regret corollary is separate and suppresses fixed problem parameters into its constant.

The source reads and proves the finite-dimensional scalar self-normalized result via conditional exponential supermartingales, a Gaussian-mixture integral, a maximal crossing bound, and an elliptical-potential determinant argument. No broader matrix self-normalized theorem is imported. The library has optional-sampling and Markov suppliers from which the finite-time crossing inequality can be derived, but no directly matching published self-normalized ellipsoid result.

findings: Sutton–Barto define a finite MDP by finite states/actions/rewards and a joint conditional law p(s',r|s,a); transition probabilities and expected rewards are marginals of this law. The scaffold keeps these finite and bounded so discounted values lie in R^S.

For 0<=gamma<1, both policy and optimality Bellman maps are sup-norm contractions with constant gamma. This fits the published Banach supplier exactly: its contraction constant is a nonnegative q with 0<=q<1, so q=gamma; no absolute-value convention is substituted.

The fixed-policy Markov-chain supplier has an explicit Axiom of Choice premise, now carried. Greedy policy improvement is source-proved for deterministic policies, but Sutton's policy-iteration pseudocode can cycle on ties (Exercise 4.4); the design requires exact evaluation and deterministic tie retention. General value-iteration convergence is cited/sketched by Sutton, so the contraction proof remains local.
